a lump sum given every

The new welfarism in India, picked up by
AAP and other parties across differentstates,
is new in two senses One, there is the tem-
porary provisioning ofa “safety net" against
what maybe termed “market failure”. For in-
stance, a lump sum given every month to
every woman from the economically weaker
sections isan adaptation of welfare to the re-
quirements of the markets.
Two, it operates beyond the NGO-centric
welfare measures and is characterised by
universal welfare benefits. In both processes,
however, this welfare gets nationalised in-
stead of socialised. The problem with such
welfarism is that it doesn't lead to the em-
powennent of the citizen; rather, it increases
the public provisioning of private goods and
cash benefits and enhances dependency. A
girl child in Delhi, for example, would want
robust democratic institutions and sustain-
able social infrastructure to enable her to ex-
ercise her socio-economic rights as freely as
any other citizen in the long run. Wecan
measure the advancement of the welfare
state in terms of state welfare recipients or
through some form of market-related pro-
vision, such as private insurance and occu-
pational welfare programmes, but we can
hardly measure the success of the welfare
state. The real problem, therefore, is the fail-
ure to effect a fully “institutional” welfare
Sate,in particular, one that addresses the is-
sue of full employment.
For the new government in Delhi, the
real challenge will beto address these lim-
itations. Govemments seldom think on a
long-term basisand are caught intheirown
web of “freebie politics”, doing more harm
than good by making the citizen passive,
dependent and disempowered over time.
In its manifesto, the BJP laid out an ambi-
tious roadmap for the city's future, giving
financial benefits to almost all sections of

society in one way or the other. In the fiscal
year 2024-25, there isa projection of rev-
enue decline from taxes, non-tax sources
and central receipts. With more than two-
thirds of revenue being utilised in the es-
tablishment and salary expenses, there
seems tobe the possibility of slippage into
deficit for the firsttime. Given such financial
conditions, the exchequer is expected to
face a heavy burden of financial accounta-
bility. For the new government, revenue
distribution might be tight, so it may have
to either divert funds from capital expen-
diture orother sectors to finance all the new
welfare schemes, or it may have to resort to
help from the Centre. It remains to be seen
how the new dispensation works on the
anthmetic to get revenues for the promised
schemes in its budget.
The citizens of Del hi have voted emphat-
ically for change. The BJP has notched upa
two-third majority in the assembly, indicat-
ing wide support not just from the disen-
chanted middleclass Thereisa rising expec-
tation from the new government for better
city governance, particularty in the areas of
pollution, safety and security, health and ed-
ucation and employment opportunities.
Delhiis unique in thatit loves politicalex-
periments. It sits atthe heart ofnational po-
itics and has enormous energy toinfluence
public discourse and national policy frame-
works, Delhi nurtures the nation’s political
and administrative capital, embraces every-
one from anywhere in the country, and at-
tracts youth from across the nation t itsuni-
versities. it enjoys extraordinary attention
and visibility. The 2025 verdict is the gover-
nance gift to the new CM, and the new gov-
emment has no option but to perform.

The writer teaches Public Policy and Politics
at the University of Dethi and is the honorary
vice-chairman at the Centre for Mutilevel

SC was right to protect Allahbadia from arrest for his crude
remarks but its gag order, call to government are disturbing
N2022, WHILE granting bailtoAt Newsco-founder Mohammed Zubair, the Supreme
Court had rejected the imposition ofa han on his social media activities, “Gag orders
have achillingeffecton the freedom of speech,” it had said. This week, the Courtap-
pears to have tumed the clock back on a right it had stoutly defended once. In pro-
hibiting podcaster-influencer Ranveer Allahbadia— whose commentsona YouTube show
Setoff acoinitOVver Sy Cailiel this Monit —and his associates fram airing content on social me-
dia until further notice, the Court hasseta troubling precedent for free speech.
The Courthasexpressed strong disapprovalofAllahbadia'scomments, asserting that
such language could bring shame to famities and society. It granted relief to Allahbadia,
inthe form of protection from arrest, besides allowing the FiRs against him to be clubbed
together. Yet, the imposition of prior restraint in the form of agagis concerning. TheCourt
must ask itselfifit wants to give fitter ammiinitian toa politicalclassthathas, inthe past,
been quick to clamp down onanything itdeems offensive, with an alacrity that cuts across
partylines. Its order also goes against the spirit that animated the Court's earlier defence
of freedom of speech, notably in Shreya Singhal vUnion of India (2015), in which theSCem-
phasised that vague restrictionson online speech can lead toa “chillingeffect”. This logic
has been upended in the Allahbadia order. The speaker is now expected to anticipate le-
gal red lines. Such restrictions can empower arbitrary state action and incentivise frivo-
jous complaints, creating anenvironment in which free expression becomes a privilege
of the powerful, not the right of the people.
It is also worrying that when hearing another matter, the Bench referred to the
Allahbadiacase and sought the government's response on wheiher it isconsidering ad-
dressing the regulatory “vacuum” inonlinecontent. Already, the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Communications and Information Technology has asked the Ministry of
Electronicsand Information Technology to look at bringingonline platformsunder legal
scrutiny. While regulation to prevent genuinely harmful content is necessary, it must be
balanced against the fundamental right to freedom of speech. Over- regulation or vague
guidelines, asthe Courtitselfhad wamed in ShreyaSinghal, could lead to self-censorship.
As the case proceeds, the Court must reconsider these directives. In anera wheredigital
platforms are the new public square, the judiciary must remain vigilant against tools of
suppression, however benign their guise and well meaning their intention.
